items.title: While You Were Sleeping: 5 stories you might have missed, Nov 7, 2026 | The Straits Times
items.excerpt: ## Trump elevates hardliner Stephen Miller as chief of staff US President Donald Trump named trusted aide Stephen Miller as his chief of staff on Nov 6, giving the architect of some of his toughest domestic policies one of the most powerful jobs in Washington after Republicans lost control of Congress. Miller, who will replace Susie Wiles, assumes the role as the president prepares to confront a Democratic-led House of Representatives and Senate and a wave of congressional investigations into his administration. A longtime proponent of expansive presidential authority, Miller takes over at a moment when the Republican Party’s defeat in the Nov 3 midterm elections could leave Trump more reliant on executive power to advance his domestic agenda. Trump said the change would take effect on Nov 9. ## Meghan’s father charged over child sex abuse photos ... Thomas Markle, the estranged father of Britain’s Duchess of Sussex, Meghan Markle, was arrested on Nov 6 on a charge of possessing child sexual abuse material, including photographs of himself with naked underage girls, found in rented storage units in California. FBI director Kash Patel said the 82-year-old father-in-law of Prince Harry was taken into custody by federal agents in Florida, where according to the Daily Mail the elder Markle, who uses a wheelchair, was a nursing home patient. If convicted, Markle could face up to 20 years in prison, the US Justice Department said. ## Europe rebuffs US drive for new ‘security architecture’ ... Europe pushed back on Nov 6 on any US efforts to rewrite the continent’s “security architecture” as part of a potential agreement with Russia to end the war in Ukraine. US President Donald Trump on Nov 5 predicted a “very big” deal with Moscow involving not only Ukraine but “all of Europe”, in remarks likely to fuel fresh fears of a pivot towards the Kremlin. At the same time, his envoy and son-in-law Jared Kushner said Washington was working on “a broader European security architecture” ahead of mediating talks next week between Ukraine and Russia in Abu Dhabi.

items.excerpt: Pope Leo begins South America 'homecoming' tour with appeal for regional unity Pope Leo urged South American countries on Friday to tackle regional issues together as he began a three-country, 12-day trip expected to draw millions across a Catholic stronghold facing sharp political divisions. The pontiff arrived in Uruguay, one of Latin America's more stable democracies, for the first stop of a ​tour that will also take him to Argentina and Peru, in one of the most demanding overseas trips by a Catholic leader in decades. Paraguay's Alliana sworn in as president after Peña impeachment Paraguayan lawmakers swore in former Vice President Pedro Alliana to lead the country ​on Friday, quickly replacing President Santiago Peña after his impeachment for alleged involvement in a bank scandal. Bomb threats warning 'the clock is ticking' disrupt TV channels across Europe Bomb threats warning "the clock ‌is ticking" were sent ​to TV stations across Europe on Friday, prompting evacuations and programming to be suspended. Warnings were sent to Irish broadcaster RTE, Britain's Sky, Bulgarian private station Nova TV and others, the companies said. No bombs were found at any affected site. RTE programmes were replaced by music and a pre-recorded message, some for as long as three hours. ... US Treasury sanctions Canadian money services firms over Iran-related transactions The US Treasury said on Friday that it had imposed financial sanctions on eight money services firms based ‌in Canada that it alleges have facilitated transactions with sanctioned Iranian entities. ... Paraguay Senate votes to impeach President Peña Paraguay's Senate on Friday voted to remove President Santiago Peña from office over his connection to the collapse of local bank ueno, which sparked a political and financial crisis and froze access to millions of accounts. Lawmakers voted in favor of Peña's dismissal in rapid impeachment proceedings despite his resignation a day earlier. ... Kenyan cult leader sentenced to 200 years in prison for mass starvation murders of children A Kenyan court sentenced cult leader Paul Mackenzie on Friday to 200 years in prison for the murders of 190 children starved to death on his orders and buried in a forest, among 500 suspected victims of one of the deadliest cult-related mass killings of modern times. The sentence comprised 100 years for murder by starvation and 100 years for direct homicide, Justice Diana Kavedza said, reading out the judgement. Four-story building collapses in Sao Paulo, four injured The roof of a four-story commercial building collapsed in the central region of Brazilian metropolis Sao Paulo on Friday, authorities said, and four people were injured. A fire department spokesperson said there had been 35 people inside the building and all of them were rescued. The four people who were injured were transported to hospitals and all are in stable condition, the spokesperson added. ... Cornell faculty senate declares no confidence in university leadership Cornell University's faculty senate approved a resolution of no confidence on Friday in the administration's ability to handle what it has called a sexual assault crisis, after a former student sued the university for not protecting her from an alleged 2024 gang rape. The resolution, which 55.6% of elected faculty senators who cast votes supported, is a condemnation of Cornell's leadership from its major legislative and advisory body, ​but has no concrete consequences. The tally showed 37% voted against it and 7.4% abstained, Cornell University spokesperson Rebecca Valli said. ... Ukraine's Zelenskiy: Russian forces plan new strikes on energy targets, bridges, infrastructure President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on Friday that intelligence showed that Russian forces were planning new strikes against key targets and the Ukrainian military was braced for a tough mission. "We have intelligence at this time that Russia is preparing new strikes on energy, on bridges across the Dnipro, on civilian infrastructure," Zelenskiy said in his nightly video address.

items.title: Fed's Mary Daly says higher interest rates 'are likely to be needed' in inflation fight
items.excerpt: Published Fri, Nov 6 2026 1:39 PM EST Updated Fri, Nov 6 2026 2:05 PM EST Jeff Cox@jeff.cox.7528@JeffCoxCNBCcom Key Points - San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly said in a CNBC interview Friday that she expects the central bank will have to raise benchmark interest rates further as it battles inflation. - On the labor market, she said Friday's jobs report was "good news for American workers" who nevertheless are seeing wages that are not keeping up with inflation. ... San Francisco Federal Reserve President Mary Daly said Friday she expects the central bank will need to raise interest rates further, but joined her fellow policymakers in saying the pace and timing remain uncertain. "My expectation is we're going to have to tighten policy further. Exactly when and how much is still to be decided because we just have to take all the variables that are coming in," Daly told CNBC's Steve Liesman during a live interview. "More is likely to be needed, and certainly ... I'm prepared to do that if that's what the economy calls for." The remarks came the same day the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that the U.S. economy added 165,000 jobs in October while the unemployment rate — the labor-market variable Fed officials focus on most — edged lower to 4.1%. Those numbers were substantially better than Wall Street expectations. Job creation, in fact, was nearly triple the Dow Jones consensus estimate. Daly called the report "good news for American workers," but noted the pressure inflation is exerting on household finances. Average hourly earnings rose 3.1% annually in October, but the September inflation rate as measured by the consumer price index was 3.7%. "They see that they can get jobs, they continue to spend. They're not out of the game, but they are on a treadmill of high inflation," she said. "This has been high for too long, almost six years, and we're really starting to feel the burden of that spread everywhere." The policymaker said she's not concerned generally about economic growth but worried about the persistence of inflation. "The job market remains stable and solid, but not booming, and you see real wages falling because those wages are not really keeping up with inflation," Daly said. "I think that's the crux of this. Good news on the jobs front, not so clear that Americans are going to gain ground in the labor market." The rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee in September increased the central bank's benchmark overnight borrowing rate by a quarter percentage point to a target range of 3.75%-4%. However, the committee last week declined to follow up that hike with another move, saying it preferred to wait for "the accumulation of more information" before deciding its next move.

items.title: Americans feel a little better, and expect less inflation | How the World Works
items.excerpt: How the World Works · 7 Nov 2026 Key takeaways ... - Long-run expectations, at 3.4%, are still well above the Fed's 2% target, so one good month is not enough. ... ## What happened The University of Michigan's index of US consumer sentiment rose to 51.0 in its preliminary November reading, published on 6 November, from 48.0 in October. Economists had expected no change. Both parts of the index improved: views of current conditions rose to 51.0 from 46.7, and expectations to 50.9 from 48.8. Sentiment is still about 10% below its level in February, before the oil shock. The inflation households expect also eased. Over the next year, they expect prices to rise 4.3%, down from 4.7% in October and the lowest since August. Over the long run, five to ten years ahead, they expect 3.4%, down from 3.5%. In February, year-ahead expectations were 3.4%. ## Why expectations matter Inflation is partly self-fulfilling. If workers expect prices to rise 4% next year, they ask for bigger pay rises; if firms expect their costs to rise, they raise prices sooner. Both make the expected inflation more likely to happen. That is why central banks watch surveys like this one closely, especially the long-run measure: a rise there would suggest people have stopped believing inflation will return to target. Two weeks ago, these expectations were at a five-month high (our story). The fall in oil prices may have helped: fuel is the price households see most often, and it shapes what they expect. ## What it means for the Fed For the Federal Reserve, it is a mixed week. October's jobs report was strong, with 165,000 new jobs, which argues for a rate rise in December. Easing inflation expectations argue for patience. Long-run expectations of 3.4% are still well above the 2% target, and above the 2.8% to 3.2% range seen in 2024.

items.title: US treasury bond prices down on Friday, Yields on 10-year, 30-year, 2-year jump. Check latest rates - The Economic Times
items.excerpt: Global Desk Last Updated: Nov 07, 2026, 05:46:00 AM IST ... US yield on the 10-year Treasury rose to 4.86 per cent from 4.84 per cent late Thursday. It had topped 5.30 per cent last month when worries about inflation, higher interest rates and rising government debt were spiking. US 30-year yields edged up 1 bp to 5.262 per cent after sliding in earlier trading to its lowest level since early September. The yield has fallen for five straight weeks. On the front end of the curve, the 2-year yield, which reflects interest rate expectations, climbed 4.7 bps to 4.524 per cent, but closed out the week with its sixth weekly decline in yield. US Treasuries fell on Friday, pushing yields higher, after the world's largest economy created far more jobs than expected last month, bolstering expectations the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates at the December policy meeting. When bond prices fall, yields rise. Despite Friday's jump, yields have steadily moved lower in recent weeks. For the week, the 10-year yield posted its fifth straight decline. **Why Did Yields Jump on Friday?** The rise in yields came after nonfarm payrolls jumped by 165,000 last month, following an upwardly revised 60,000 gain for September, the US Labor Department said. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast payrolls advancing 65,000 after a previously reported 29,000 increase in September. On one hand, the encouraging data could mean the US economy may be able to absorb a slowdown in construction of AI data centres. But at the same time, the strong growth in jobs could push upward on inflation. Following the report, traders saw a greater probability of the Federal Reserve hiking its short-term interest rate at its next meeting in December, according to data from CME Group. Rate hikes by the Fed can rein in inflation, but they do so by making borrowing money more expensive for everyone and slowing the overall economy.

Miller, long a key member of Trump’s inner circle, is a key architect of the administration’s hard-line immigration policies. Wiles, a steely political operator and the first woman to serve in the post, was Trump’s longest-serving White House chief of staff and his longtime adviser. A handful of remaining Senate and House races still to be called by The Associated Press will determine the strength of Democrats’ majority in Congress. Democrats will hold at least 54 seats in the 100-member Senate next year and as many as 56 depending on final results in Alaska and Mississippi — where contests remain narrow with votes still outstanding. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, who is likely to return as majority leader next year, promised in an interview with the AP that Democrats will prevent the Republican president from installing a “right-winger” on the Supreme Court or “crappy nominees” elsewhere in the federal judiciary or in Trump’s Cabinet. ... ### US Department of Justice drops lawsuit over 20,000 California ballots The U.S. Department of Justice has moved to dismiss its own lawsuit that aimed to stop California from processing up to 20,000 ballots it suspected were mailed to noncitizens. The federal government’s decision comes before a scheduled hearing next week where a special master was to evaluate the list’s accuracy. California officials and a federal judge have said the list is outdated and includes legitimate voters. The lawsuit was part of the Trump administration’s effort to stop alleged illegal voting. ... ### After Democrats flip Texas House, state’s longest-serving Black lawmaker says she has support for ... Senfronia Thompson would be the first Black lawmaker and first woman elevated to Texas House speaker in the state’s history. The 87-year-old Democrat was first elected in 1972. Democrats won a majority in the state House for the first time since 2002 as part of their sweeping victories in Tuesday’s midterm elections.

items.excerpt: By AP Published On 7 Nov 2026 7 Nov 2026 US President Donald Trump has confirmed US military strikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island, claiming that Washington has made “a lot of progress” in talks with Iran. Trump said on Friday that US forces had carried out what he described as minor strikes against Iranian air defence systems. “We do minor strikes,” Trump told reporters in West Palm Beach, Florida. “They knocked out – they built a little bit of an anti-aircraft device, and we knocked it out in about 15 minutes, maybe five.” Trump spoke shortly after Iranian state media reported two missile strikes in the Suza area of Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial route for oil shipments. State broadcaster IRIB also reported an Iranian army statement, saying that the country’s air defence forces intercepted and destroyed an American MQ-9 drone over Qeshm Island. In response to reports of explosions heard on Iran’s Qeshm Island, US Central Command (CENTCOM), which oversees US military operations in the Middle East, said the situation is “relatively calm”. A CENTCOM official told Al Jazeera that they are aware of the reports, adding they have no further comment. CENTCOM announced in a post on X late on Friday that the US “is offering a reward of up to $20 million and possible relocation for information about Iran’s nuclear program, including its facilities, equipment, and associated personnel, such as those in the scientific community, or the movement of any of the above”. On Monday, Iranian media reported several explosions on Qeshm Island, as American media outlets reported that the US military carried out what officials called “ defensive strikes” in the Strait of Hormuz. ## Ongoing talks Trump told reporters several times on Friday that his administration was talking to representatives from Tehran. “We’re dealing with them now. They want to make a deal,” the US president said. “We’ve made a lot of progress with Iran,” he added, without providing details. On Saturday, Qatar dismissed reports claiming negotiations between the US and Iran have failed, warning that such claims benefit “only those seeking to prolong the war”. “Promoting such false claims serves only those seeking to prolong the war and destabilise the region,” said Majed al-Ansari, spokesperson for the Qatari Ministry of Foreign Affairs, in a post on X. Friday’s strikes are the first since Trump’s Republican Party was dealt a blow in Tuesday’s midterm elections in the US. Trump blamed the election results on the Iran war. Since Tuesday’s midterm elections, Trump has shifted between threatening Iran and suggesting that a resolution to the war is near. On Thursday, Trump said the US may have to “destroy” the rest of Iran, adding that people will “know soon enough” if he acts. Unnamed Pentagon officials and military commanders told The New York Times on Wednesday that thousands of US air and naval forces on more than a dozen ships and at bases around the Middle East and in the US are poised to resume major combat operations against Iran on Trump’s orders. Tehran has stepped up diplomatic efforts amid suggestions from Trump that the US could resume full-scale strikes on Iran.

items.excerpt: - AP - Nov 6, 2026 - Nov 6, 2026 Updated 2 hrs ago Meghan's estranged father arrested and charged with possessing child sexual abuse materials TAMPA, Fla. (AP) — Thomas Markle, the 82-year-old father of Prince Harry’s wife Meghan, has been arrested by federal agents in Florida and charged with possessing child sexual abuse material in California. Thomas Markle was released after a court appearance in Tampa. Authorities say a search of storage units in the Los Angeles area turned up dozens of items. There was no immediate comment from his lawyer. Meghan Markle had recently said she's “deeply distressed” about allegations that a collection of child sexual abuse images were found at her father’s former home in the Philippines. NEW YORK (AP) — Britney Spears' 2001 self-titled album ‘Britney' marked a pivotal moment in her career. At 19, she was already a global icon, transitioning from teen pop to a more mature sound. The album, certified quadruple platinum, showcased her evolution with hits like “I'm a Slave 4 U.” On Friday, Legacy Recordings releases the “Britney (25th Anniversary Edition).” It features five previously unreleased tracks and two new remixes. These songs add depth to her legacy, reflecting themes of autonomy and self-definition. Fans can revisit the album, exploring its impact and Spears’ journey from adolescence to adulthood. NEW YORK (AP) — Awkwafina has taken a surprising turn in her career by diving into the culinary world. Her new Apple TV series, “Awkwafina: The Unlikely Cook,” follows her journey from a novice cook to opening her own restaurant. The show, premiering Friday, captures her learning experiences, from making stir-fry to mastering Peking duck. Awkwafina was born Nora Lum and comes from a family with a rich restaurant history. They opened the New York City eatery Lum's. Her journey reconnects her with her roots and honors her family. The series also highlights a trend of Asian Americans returning to the restaurant industry, defying their parents' expectations. NEW YORK (AP) — Siân Heder's follow-up to the best picture-winning “CODA” chronicles the disability rights pioneer Judy Heumann. Heumann died at the age of 75 in 2023 while Heder was developing the movie with her. She resolved to push on with the project to honor Heumann and try to bring some of her accessibility gains to the movie industry. Characters with disabilities remain extremely uncommon in Hollywood productions, and big-screen biopics like “Being Heumann” are even more seldom. “Being Heumann,” starring Ruth Madeley as Heumann, features the largest ensemble ever of performers with disabilities. SANTIAGO, Chile (AP) — Oscar-winning Chilean filmmaker Sebastián Lelio has died in Santiago, Chile, at 52. His family announced his death Friday on Instagram, citing health reasons but not specifying the cause. Lelio was known for his groundbreaking film “A Fantastic Woman,” which portrayed a transgender woman and won the Academy Award for best international film. It was Chile's second Oscar win. Lelio’s other works include "Gloria," "The Wonder," and “Disobedience.” He had begun filming “Poeta Chileno” in September. Born in Argentina, Lelio moved to Chile at age two and studied at the Chilean Film School. ... VENICE, Italy (AP) — South Korean filmmaker Lee Chang-dong's latest film, “Possible Love,” is now streaming on Netflix. The film explores the impact of mass layoffs in South Korea, inspired by the 2009 Ssangyong Motor Co. incident. The story follows a laid-off autoworker and his wife, played by Jeon Do-yeon, who agrees to be followed by a well-off documentary filmmaker. The film, which premiered at the Venice Film Festival where it won the runner-up prize, is South Korea’s submission for the Academy Awards. Lee last directed “Burning,” which was short-listed for an Oscar in 2018. NEW YORK (AP) — Lady Gaga, Shakira, Pink, Boy George, Jack White, Sia, Vince Gill, Ne-Yo, Blondie’s Debbie Harry and Chris Stein are among the impressive list of nominees for the 2027 Songwriters Hall of Fame class. Also on the ballot are America’s Gerry Beckley and Dewey Bunnell, Grandmaster Melle Mel as well as members of ZZ Top and War. Eligible voting members have until midnight Eastern Standard Time on Dec. 14 to turn in ballots with their choices of up to three nominees from the songwriter category and up to three from the performing-songwriter category. The 2027 inductees will be announced in early 2027. Last year's class included Taylor Swift, Kiss’s Gene Simmons, Paul Stanley and more.

items.excerpt: # Melbourne Recital Centre: Nat Bartsch – Acceptance Does Not Mean Surrender ## 7 November @ 8:30 pm - 9:30 pm AEDT A powerful musical response to our climate crisis. Celebrate the release of award-winning pianist and composer Nat Bartsch’s tenth album, Acceptance Does Not Mean Surrender, a powerful musical response to our climate crisis. Inspired by conversations with eight climate scientists, hear their voices embedded in Nat’s evocative works, along with sounds of nature and stunning cinematography of the natural environment by Stefan Raabe. Joined by Nat’s ARIA-nominated jazz quartet and members of Monash Art Ensemble, each movement guides listeners through themes that emerged from Nat’s research, offering a space to process climate grief, connect with nature, and cultivate resilience. ‘I hope this piece will also inspire you to find ways to do what you can for climate action; to connect with nature, listen to the science, process some challenging emotions, and find beauty in broken places.’ – Nat Bartsch
